blocks.body:
Two speed cameras on a motorway are $30$ km apart, and a car passes them $15$ minutes apart. Its average speed was $120$ km/h, and the driver gets a fine for exceeding $110$ km/h, although neither camera saw the car going that fast. The authorities are relying on a theorem: if the average speed over a journey was $120$ km/h, then at some instant the speedometer read exactly $120$.

That theorem is the mean value theorem. It sounds obvious, yet it is the key to almost every fact linking a function with its derivative: that a function with zero derivative is constant, that a positive derivative means increasing, error bounds for approximations, L'Hôpital's rule and Taylor's theorem. Its proof is short but depends on the extreme value theorem, which in turn rests on the completeness of the real numbers.

blocks.title: The picture
blocks.body:
Draw the graph of $f$ over $[a, b]$ and the chord joining its two endpoints. The chord has slope
$$m = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a},$$
the average rate of change of $f$ over the interval. Now slide a ruler parallel to the chord, starting on the chord and moving towards a side on which part of the graph lies (if the graph is the chord itself, every point will do), and stop just before it leaves the graph for good. At that last moment it touches the graph at some point $c$ strictly between $a$ and $b$ without crossing it, and there it is a tangent line, so $f'(c) = m$.

For a concrete case take $f(x) = x^3$ on $[0, 2]$. The average slope is $\frac{8 - 0}{2} = 4$, and $f'(c) = 3c^2 = 4$ when $c = 2/\sqrt3 \approx 1.155$, which does lie in $(0, 2)$. Usually $c$ cannot be computed so easily, and the theorem never says where it is; it only guarantees that it exists. That is enough for all the applications.

blocks.title: Interior extremum theorem (Fermat)
blocks.body: Let $f$ be defined on an interval $I$, and suppose $f$ has a local maximum or a local minimum at a point $c$ in the interior of $I$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then $f'(c) = 0$.

Suppose $c$ is a local maximum: there is $\delta > 0$ such that $(c - \delta, c + \delta) \subseteq I$ and $f(c + h) \le f(c)$ whenever $|h| < \delta$. For $0 < h < \delta$ the difference quotient $\dfrac{f(c + h) - f(c)}{h}$ is $\le 0$, since its numerator is $\le 0$ and its denominator is positive; so its limit as $h \to 0^+$, which is $f'(c)$, is $\le 0$. For $-\delta < h < 0$ the quotient is $\ge 0$, so $f'(c) \ge 0$. Hence $f'(c) = 0$. For a local minimum apply this to $-f$.

blocks.title: Rolle's theorem
blocks.body: Let $f$ be continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$, with $f(a) = f(b)$. Then there is a point $c \in (a, b)$ with $f'(c) = 0$.

By the extreme value theorem, a standard result that we quote without proof, a function continuous on a closed bounded interval $[a, b]$ attains a largest value $M$ and a smallest value $m$ on it; this is where the completeness of the real numbers enters (see [[continuity]] and [[compactness]]). If $M = m$, then $f$ is constant and $f'(c) = 0$ for every $c \in (a, b)$. Otherwise at least one of $M$ and $m$ differs from the common endpoint value $f(a) = f(b)$, so it is attained at some point $c$ strictly inside $(a, b)$. Then $c$ is a maximum or minimum of $f$ at an interior point where $f$ is differentiable, so $f'(c) = 0$ by Fermat's theorem.

blocks.title: Mean value theorem
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$. Then there is a point $c \in (a, b)$ with
$$f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}.$$

Let $m$ be the slope of the chord, and subtract the chord from $f$:
$$g(x) = f(x) - f(a) - m(x - a).$$
Then $g$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$, with $g(a) = 0$ and $g(b) = f(b) - f(a) - m(b - a) = 0$. By Rolle's theorem $g'(c) = 0$ for some $c \in (a, b)$, and $g'(c) = f'(c) - m$.

blocks.title: What the derivative says about the function
blocks.body:
Here is why the theorem matters. Let $f$ be differentiable on an interval $I$. For any $x < y$ in $I$, the mean value theorem on $[x, y]$ gives
$$f(y) - f(x) = f'(c)\,(y - x) \quad \text{for some } c \in (x, y).$$
Reading off the sign or size of $f'(c)$:

1. If $f' = 0$ on $I$, then $f(y) = f(x)$: $f$ is constant. Hence two functions with the same derivative on an interval differ by a constant.
2. If $f' > 0$ on $I$, then $f(y) > f(x)$: $f$ is strictly increasing. If $f' \ge 0$, then $f$ is non-decreasing. Similarly for negative derivatives.
3. If $|f'| \le M$ on $I$, then $|f(y) - f(x)| \le M|y - x|$.

The same conclusions hold on a closed interval $[a, b]$ if $f$ is only assumed continuous at the endpoints and the condition on $f'$ holds on $(a, b)$. The word interval is essential: $f(x) = x/|x|$ has derivative $0$ at every point of its domain $\mathbb R \setminus \{0\}$, but it is not constant. And the converse of statement 2 fails: $x^3$ is strictly increasing although its derivative vanishes at $0$.

blocks.title: Cauchy's mean value theorem
blocks.body:
Let $f$ and $g$ be continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$. Then there is a point $c \in (a, b)$ with
$$\big(f(b) - f(a)\big)\,g'(c) = \big(g(b) - g(a)\big)\,f'(c).$$
If $g'$ has no zero in $(a, b)$, this can be written $\dfrac{f(b) - f(a)}{g(b) - g(a)} = \dfrac{f'(c)}{g'(c)}$.

Let $$h(x) = \big(f(b) - f(a)\big)g(x) - \big(g(b) - g(a)\big)f(x)$$. Expanding, $h(a) = f(b)g(a) - g(b)f(a)$ and $h(b) = f(b)g(a) - g(b)f(a)$ as well, so Rolle's theorem gives a point $c \in (a, b)$ with $h'(c) = 0$, which is the claim. If $g'$ never vanishes on $(a, b)$, then $g(b) \ne g(a)$ (otherwise Rolle's theorem applied to $g$ would produce a zero of $g'$), so we may divide.

Taking $g(x) = x$ recovers the ordinary mean value theorem. Geometrically, Cauchy's version is the ordinary one for the curve $t \mapsto (g(t), f(t))$ in the plane: some tangent to the curve is parallel to the chord.

blocks.title: Estimating a square root
blocks.solution:
Apply the mean value theorem to $f(x) = \sqrt x$ on $[100, 101]$. For some $c \in (100, 101)$,
$$\sqrt{101} - \sqrt{100} = f'(c)\cdot 1 = \frac{1}{2\sqrt c}.$$
Since $100 < c < 101 < 121$, we have $10 < \sqrt c < 11$, so $\frac{1}{22} < \frac{1}{2\sqrt c} < \frac{1}{20}$. Adding $10$ gives the claim. Indeed $\sqrt{101} = 10.0498\ldots$, while $10 + \frac{1}{22} = 10.0454\ldots$ and $10 + \frac{1}{20} = 10.05$.

The theorem converts a bound on the derivative into a bound on the function. This is how most error estimates in calculus are proved.

blocks.title: Exactly one root
blocks.body: Show that the equation $x^5 + x - 1 = 0$ has exactly one real solution.
blocks.solution:
Existence. The polynomial $p(x) = x^5 + x - 1$ is continuous with $p(0) = -1 < 0$ and $p(1) = 1 > 0$, so by the intermediate value theorem ([[continuity]]) it has a root in $(0, 1)$.

Uniqueness. Suppose $p(r) = p(s) = 0$ with $r < s$. By Rolle's theorem $p'(c) = 0$ for some $c \in (r, s)$. But $p'(x) = 5x^4 + 1 \ge 1$ for every $x$, a contradiction. So the root is unique.

The same argument shows more generally that between two zeros of a differentiable function there is a zero of its derivative. So if $f'$ has $k$ zeros on an interval, then $f$ has at most $k + 1$ there. In particular, if a polynomial of degree $n$ has $n$ distinct real roots, its derivative has $n - 1$ distinct real roots, one strictly between each consecutive pair.

blocks.title: A root from an averaging condition
blocks.body:
Let $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n$ be real numbers with
$$a_0 + \frac{a_1}{2} + \frac{a_2}{3} + \dots + \frac{a_n}{n + 1} = 0.$$
Show that the polynomial $a_0 + a_1x + \dots + a_nx^n$ has a root in $(0, 1)$.
blocks.solution:
The condition looks like the value of something at $x = 1$. Consider
$$F(x) = a_0x + \frac{a_1}{2}x^2 + \dots + \frac{a_n}{n + 1}x^{n+1},$$
chosen so that $F'(x) = a_0 + a_1x + \dots + a_nx^n$. Then $F(0) = 0$, and $F(1) = 0$ by hypothesis. As a polynomial, $F$ is continuous and differentiable everywhere, so Rolle's theorem on $[0, 1]$ gives $c \in (0, 1)$ with $F'(c) = 0$.

The idea to remember: to show that an expression $P$ has a root, look for a function $F$ whose derivative is $P$ (or $P$ times something that never vanishes, such as $e^xP$) and which takes equal values at two points.

blocks.body:
- Both hypotheses matter. $f(x) = |x|$ on $[-1, 1]$ is continuous with average slope $0$, but $f'(c)$ is never $0$: differentiability fails at a single interior point. And $f(x) = x$ for $0 \le x < 1$ with $f(1) = 0$ is differentiable on $(0, 1)$ with $f(0) = f(1)$, yet $f' = 1$ throughout: continuity fails at an endpoint.
- The point $c$ is usually not unique, and the theorem gives no formula for it. A proof may use only the fact that $c \in (a, b)$.
- Conclusions such as "$f' = 0$ implies $f$ is constant" need an interval, as $x/|x|$ shows.
- The theorem is false for complex-valued or vector-valued functions. For $f(t) = \cos t + i\sin t$ on $[0, 2\pi]$ the average rate of change is $0$, while $|f'(t)| = 1$ for every $t$. What survives is the inequality $|f(b) - f(a)| \le (b - a)\sup|f'|$.
- A positive derivative at a single point is not enough for monotonicity near that point. The function $f(x) = x + 2x^2\sin(1/x)$, $f(0) = 0$, has $f'(0) = 1$, but $f'(x) = -1$ at every point $x = \frac{1}{2k\pi}$, so $f$ is not increasing on any interval around $0$.

The consequences above are the basis of [[deriv-applications]]: sign charts for $f'$ and $f''$, and the first and second derivative tests. Cauchy's version is exactly what is needed to prove [[lhopital]]. Applying Rolle's theorem repeatedly to a cleverly chosen auxiliary function gives [[taylor]] with the Lagrange form of the remainder, of which the mean value theorem is the degree-zero case. In [[ftc]] the mean value theorem shows that $\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)$.

The Lipschitz bound $|f(x) - f(y)| \le M|x - y|$ is the estimate behind uniqueness of solutions of differential equations ([[ode-first]]). For complex-valued functions only the inequality form survives, and for [[holomorphic]] functions it is usually proved by writing $f(b) - f(a)$ as an integral of $f'$ along the segment.

1. Show that $|\sin x - \sin y| \le |x - y|$ for all real $x$ and $y$.
2. Show that $\dfrac{x}{1 + x} < \ln(1 + x) < x$ for every $x > 0$.
3. Suppose $f$ is differentiable on $\mathbb R$, $f(0) = 1$ and $f'(x) = 2x$ for all $x$. Prove that $f(x) = x^2 + 1$.
4. Suppose $f$ is twice differentiable on $\mathbb R$ and has three distinct zeros. Show that $f''$ has at least one zero.
